subject: Modern History
name: History Revolutions, Units 3 and 4
about: VCE, American, French, Russian and Chinese revolutions
syllabus: VCE History Study Design (from 2022), Revolutions Units 3 and 4

points.title: The colonies before 1763
points.brief: Thirteen British colonies largely governed themselves through elected assemblies and grew wealthy through trade.

points.title: The French and Indian War
points.brief: Britain's victory over France in North America by 1763 left it in debt, so it looked to the colonies to pay for their defence.

points.title: British policy after 1763
points.brief: Trade rules, the Proclamation line limiting western settlement and new taxes showed tighter British control of the colonies.

points.title: Taxation without representation
points.brief: Colonists objected to taxes such as the Stamp Act, passed by a parliament in which they had no members.

points.title: The Boston Tea Party and the Coercive Acts
points.brief: Colonists destroyed taxed tea in 1773, and Britain answered with laws that colonists called the Intolerable Acts.

points.title: Enlightenment ideas in America
points.brief: Ideas of natural rights and government by consent, from writers such as Locke and Paine, shaped colonial thinking.

points.title: Leaders of the American cause
points.brief: George III, George Washington, Samuel Adams, John Hancock, Thomas Paine and Thomas Jefferson each shaped the road to independence.

points.title: Popular movements in America
points.brief: The Patriots, the Sons and Daughters of Liberty, Committees of Correspondence and Provincial Congresses organised colonists against British rule.

points.title: The Declaration of Independence
points.brief: In 1776 the Continental Congress declared the colonies independent, listing grievances against the king.

points.title: Winning the war
points.brief: With help from France, the Continental Army defeated Britain, which recognised independence in the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

points.title: The Articles of Confederation
points.brief: The first national government was weak, unable to tax or control trade, which led to calls for change.

points.title: Shays' Rebellion
points.brief: A revolt of indebted farmers in 1786 and 1787 showed the weakness of the national government and pushed leaders to change it.

points.title: The Constitution of 1787
points.brief: A new constitution created a federal government with separated powers and checks and balances.

points.title: The Bill of Rights
points.brief: The first ten amendments protected rights such as freedom of speech and religion.

points.title: Leaders of the new nation
points.brief: George Washington, Alexander Hamilton, Patrick Henry and James Madison shaped the new government and argued over its powers.

points.title: Who the revolution left out
points.brief: Loyalists lost homes and land, while enslaved people, women and Native Americans gained little, and slavery continued in much of the new nation.

points.title: Change and continuity in America
points.brief: Between 1754 and 1789 government changed greatly, but much of society, including slavery, stayed the same.

points.title: The Old Regime
points.brief: French society was split into three estates, with the clergy and nobles holding privileges and the Third Estate paying most taxes.

points.title: Royal debt and financial crisis
points.brief: Wars, including aid to the American Revolution, left the crown nearly bankrupt by the 1780s.

points.title: The crisis of 1787 and 1788
points.brief: The nobles' revolt against tax reform and protests such as the Day of Tiles forced the king to call the Estates-General.

points.title: Enlightenment ideas in France
points.brief: Writers such as Rousseau and Voltaire questioned absolute monarchy, privilege and the church.

points.title: Leaders before the revolution
points.brief: Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, the writer Sieyès, Lafayette and the finance minister Necker shaped the crisis.

points.title: The Estates-General of 1789
points.brief: Called to solve the crisis, it deadlocked over voting until the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly.

points.title: The fall of the Bastille
points.brief: On 14 July 1789 Parisians stormed the Bastille, showing the crown had lost control of the capital.

points.title: Peasants, workers and the Great Fear
points.brief: Hungry Parisian workers and peasants who attacked noble estates in mid-1789 pushed the revolution further.

points.title: The end of feudal privilege
points.brief: In August 1789 the Assembly abolished feudal dues and noble privileges.

points.title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man
points.brief: The 1789 declaration proclaimed liberty, equality before the law and the sovereignty of the nation.

points.title: The October Days
points.brief: In October 1789 Parisian women marched to Versailles and brought the royal family back to Paris.

points.title: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy
points.brief: The state's reform of the church split the clergy and turned many Catholics against the revolution.

points.title: The end of the monarchy
points.brief: After the king's failed flight in 1791 and war with Austria, the monarchy fell in 1792 and Louis XVI was executed in 1793.

points.title: The Terror
points.brief: The Committee of Public Safety used mass arrests and executions in 1793 and 1794 to defend the revolution.

points.title: Leaders of the revolution
points.brief: Danton, Marat and Robespierre led the radical revolution, and Robespierre drove the Terror until his own execution in 1794.

points.title: The revolution and ordinary people
points.brief: Peasants, sans-culottes and women took part in and were changed by the revolution, but gains were uneven.

points.title: Change and continuity in France
points.brief: Between 1774 and 1795 privilege and absolute monarchy ended, but many hopes for equality were not met.

points.title: Tsarist autocracy
points.brief: Nicholas II ruled with near-total power, backed by the army, the church and secret police.

points.title: Social and economic conditions
points.brief: Most Russians were poor peasants, while fast industrial growth crowded workers into harsh city conditions.

points.title: The 1905 Revolution
points.brief: Defeat by Japan and Bloody Sunday sparked strikes and revolts, and the October Manifesto created the Duma, which the tsar later limited.

points.title: Reform and reaction
points.brief: Stolypin's land reforms and harsh repression between 1906 and 1914 failed to settle the empire.

points.title: Revolutionary ideas
points.brief: Liberal ideas, Marxism and Lenin's idea of a party leading the workers challenged the tsar's rule.

points.title: Revolutionary parties
points.brief: The Bolsheviks, Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries offered different paths to change.

points.title: The First World War and Russia
points.brief: Defeats, huge losses and food shortages destroyed support for the tsar.

points.title: The tsar, the tsarina and Rasputin
points.brief: Nicholas II, Alexandra and Rasputin's influence at court damaged the monarchy's standing during the war.

points.title: The February Revolution
points.brief: In February 1917 strikes and a mutiny in Petrograd forced Nicholas II to give up the throne.

points.title: The Provisional Government and the Soviets
points.brief: Power was shared between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet, in an uneasy dual power.

points.title: The October Revolution
points.brief: In October 1917 Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd.

points.title: The first Bolshevik decrees
points.brief: Decrees on land and peace gave land to peasants and sought an end to the war.

points.title: The Constituent Assembly
points.brief: The Bolsheviks shut down the elected assembly in January 1918 after other parties won most seats.

points.title: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
points.brief: In 1918 Russia left the war, giving up large territories to Germany.

points.title: The Civil War
points.brief: The Reds fought the Whites and others from 1918 to 1921, and the Bolsheviks won.

points.title: War Communism and the Red Terror
points.brief: The Bolsheviks took grain, ran industry and used terror against opponents, causing famine and revolt.

points.title: The New Economic Policy
points.brief: In 1921 Lenin allowed some private trade to revive the economy.

points.title: Building a one-party state
points.brief: By the mid-1920s the Communist Party had banned other parties and controlled the state.

points.title: Leaders of the new state
points.brief: Lenin, Trotsky, Dzerzhinsky of the Cheka and Alexandra Kollontai shaped Soviet Russia in its first years.

points.title: Change and continuity in Russia
points.brief: Between 1896 and 1927 the tsar was replaced, but one-party rule and a secret police kept older patterns of power.

points.title: The early Republic
points.brief: After the Qing fell in 1912, Yuan Shikai took power and tried to make himself emperor, and the Republic failed to unite China.

points.title: The warlord era
points.brief: After 1916 China split among regional warlords, with no strong central government.

points.title: The May Fourth Movement
points.brief: The New Culture Movement and the 1919 protests against the Treaty of Versailles fed nationalism and interest in new ideas, including communism.

points.title: The Guomindang and the Communists
points.brief: Sun Yixian's Three Principles guided the Nationalists, who worked with the Communists until Jiang Jieshi turned on them in the 1927 Shanghai Massacre.

points.title: The Long March
points.brief: In 1934 and 1935 the Communists retreated thousands of kilometres, and Mao Zedong rose to lead them.

points.title: Mao Zedong Thought
points.brief: Mao adapted communism to China, putting peasants rather than city workers at the centre of revolution.

points.title: The war against Japan
points.brief: Japan's invasion weakened the Nationalists, while the Communists grew strong among peasants.

points.title: The Civil War and 1949
points.brief: The Communists defeated the Nationalists and proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949.

points.title: Land reform
points.brief: Land was taken from landlords and given to peasants, often with violence against landlords.

points.title: Thought reform and mass campaigns
points.brief: Campaigns such as the Three Antis and Five Antis targeted officials, business owners and critics in the early 1950s.

points.title: The first Five-Year Plan
points.brief: Soviet-style planning built heavy industry in the 1950s.

points.title: The Hundred Flowers Campaign
points.brief: Mao invited criticism in 1956 and 1957, then punished many critics in the Anti-Rightist Campaign.

points.title: The Great Leap Forward
points.brief: A drive from 1958 to industrialise fast through communes led to a famine in which millions died.

points.title: The Cultural Revolution
points.brief: From 1966 Mao encouraged Red Guards to attack officials and old culture, causing chaos and persecution.

points.title: Leaders of the People's Republic
points.brief: Mao, Lin Biao, Liu Shaoqi and Jiang Qing struggled over the direction of the new state.

points.title: Change and continuity in China
points.brief: Between 1912 and 1976 landlords and the old elite lost power, but one-party rule and hardship for many continued.
